fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes hot-deformation DRV/DRX for the target mechanism of vacancy-assisted Shockley-partial nucleation and stacking-fault-mediated plasticity.
The proposed strain-rate range of 0.001–0.1 s^-1 is wholly outside the simulated 10^8–10^10 s^-1 regime.
It assumes grain-boundary migration and recrystallized grain formation despite the target being a periodic FCC single crystal without an initial grain-boundary network.
It omits the controlled crystallographic-orientation comparison, including the predicted maximum yield stress along <-111>.
It predicts strain-rate-dependent peak strength, whereas the target result is negligible yield-strength sensitivity to strain rate, coupled to increased dislocation density and flow stress.

The cited evidence concerns hot compression of compositionally different, Co-containing and C/Mo-alloyed HEAs at 800–1000 degrees C, so it does not substantiate the proposed mechanism in equiatomic Co-free FeNiCrMn under the target conditions.
explanation: The response addresses temperature and strain-rate effects and supplies a falsifiable microscopy-based experiment, but it reconstructs a fundamentally different physical regime. Its DRV/DRX model could be examined in a hot-worked polycrystalline alloy, yet it is not applicable to the target periodic single-crystal molecular-dynamics system at 10–600 K and ultrahigh strain rates. The expected target comparison is tensile loading by crystallographic orientation, temperature, and rate relative to 300 K and 10^9 s^-1, with stress-drop, DXA, and CNA analyses distinguishing Shockley-partial/stacking-fault plasticity from phase transformation. The response neither predicts the <-111> anisotropy nor the rate-insensitive yield strength, and its supporting literature is transferred across major composition, loading-mode, temperature, timescale, and microstructure differences.
